A computer-use agent can perform embodied tasks by observing the environment rendered on a screen and interacting with it through software. The observations include physical environments such as camera images of scenes, 3D scans, or changes in rooms and viewpoints within the world that keeps moving. Actions involve manipulating these environments using controls provided by the software, which includes actions like moving (move( , x, y, z, θ)), opening or closing a gripper, clicking on screen elements such as buttons, menus, windows, and typing commands.

The exact method is described in Excerpt 3 (Paper ID: 2611.09847, Page: 5-6). The software for each competition was built to render the agent's view of a physical environment on a screen and provide controls for acting within it. This shared agent design allows the same computer-use agent to perform tasks across different embodied AI tasks by changing only the specific software used in each competition.

The baseline is that these tasks can be formulated as interactions with digital software, which lets us apply the same methods for training agents to perform these interactions (Excerpt 2, Paper ID: 2611.09847, Page: 2). The limitations are not explicitly stated in the provided excerpts but could include differences in specific hardware or software configurations required by each competition and potential variations in how tasks are defined across different embodied AI environments.

retrieval_meta.search_query: What is the role of B-spline reparameterization in FlowMoP?

generation.answer: In FlowMoP, B-spline reparameterization is used to compress future motion predictions into fewer control points while enforcing C2 temporal smoothness. This method involves using cubic B-splines for both trajectory (Ct control points) and pose (Cp control points). The reparameterization is applied by constructing a clamped knot vector with n = C −d −1 uniformly spaced interior knots, where d = 3 in this case. The role of B-spline reparameterization is to operate entirely in control-point space and project velocity residuals to full resolution via a fixed basis matrix for temporally-weighted supervision. This approach allows the model to handle structured skeleton prediction within a flow matching model, offering advantages similar to those exploited here. It represents the first application of B-spline reparameterization to generative 3D motion prediction.

generation.answer: The training adjustment used to mitigate Laya's option-order sensitivity is shuffling the options during fine-tuning. This method is described in Excerpt 2 (Paper ID: 2611.09803, Page: 2-3). Shuffled fine-tuning on a few thousand teacher-verified rows reduces Laya’s order-sensitive questions from 25.8% to 7.2%. The exact shuffling and vote for high-stakes decisions is also mentioned in Excerpt 4 (Paper ID: 2611.09803, Page: 2), where it is stated that the parallel layout is a principled fix when training from scratch. This adaptation of the base checkpoint to the parallel layout gives a flip rate of 0.5%. Therefore, both shuffling options during fine-tuning and using the parallel layout are used as mitigation strategies for Laya's option-order sensitivity.

They are simple and publicly motivated, and we think measurement is more useful to defenders than harmful to them. 18  Conclusion Laya’s released checkpoints are order-sensitive on realistic questions: 25.8% of questions flip when only the option order changes. Why a separate study for a non-generative modelThe mitigations proposed for generative models, such as debiasing the prior over option IDs, assume a probability distribution over answer tokens. Laya has no such distribution: it has one scalar logit per slot. The relevant questions are therefore different: is the logit a function of the option text alone, or of its position? Is the dependence learned from the training order or built into the positional machinery of the encoder? The identical-option probe (Section 6) and the layout comparison (Section 7) answer these two questions separately. Evaluation protocol

Contributions(i) On the base checkpoint 25.8% [22.9–28.7] of questions change their answer purely because the options were reordered (19.7% on the 605 English-language items alone). (ii) The dependence is not a first/last artefact alone: the first-vs-last accuracy gap is 10.1%, but predictions are concentrated in particular slots (total-variation distance from uniform 0.09 at K=3, 0.07 at K=12). (iii) Fine-tuning with shuffling reduces the flip rate to 7.2%, whereas the same rows without shuffling give 11.4%
